newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ANALYSTS LOOK TO BOONSTRA FOR NEW PHILIPS STRATEGY.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS LOOK TO BOONSTRA FOR NEW PHILIPS STRATEGY.

text.p: When Cor Boonstra takes the reins at Philips Electronics on Tuesday analysts will be looking for signs he can blow away the perception of Europe's biggest consumer electronics firm as a lumbering, unfocused giant.
Analysts say Boonstra needs new strategies to build on the achievements of outgoing chairman Jan Timmer, who dragged Philips from the brink of financial disaster in the early 1990s.
Boonstra, with a track record of vigorous restructuring, might take an axe to costs but that may not be enough to convince analysts Philips has a winning formula for the future.

"The main question in my view is does he have any different strategic views? Will he look beyond cost cutting to finding new growth areas apart from Asia, also maybe (find) new activities or new alliances?" said Joost van Beek of Van Meer James Capel.
"Strategy," said Van Beek. "That's what I'm most curious about. I'm not interested in cost-cutting."
"It's very clear in this market if you want to win you have to include alliances, like in the DVD (digital video disc) area where you have to find compromises," he added.

Analysts agree Philips is a far cry from the slow-moving unprofitable leviathan of the early 1990s, with more clearly defined management structures and a much greater commitment to developing and delivering goods that consumers actually want.

But does the company now need a a re-run of Timmer's Centurion plan, which hauled Philips from losses of 4.2 billion guilders in 1990 to 1995's profit of 2.5 billion guilders and shed 60,000 jobs from Philips' then 310,000 payroll?
Analysts anticipate Boonstra might have a certain level of restructuring in mind and the determination to dish out more harsh medicine, but they want more than that.

"I guess what people are half expecting, half hoping...is that Philips needs to sharpen up a bit, in general terms. On non-performing businesses and maybe in marketing terms," said London-based Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean.

"The whole idea of getting businesses to perform the way they should, finding clear growth areas, setting clear strategies and enhancing shareholder value, those are the kind of things people are looking for," said Dean.
Boonstra, 58, the son of a grocery store owner from the northern Dutch province of Friesland, is said by Philips insiders to be fiercely committed to value for shareholders.
"He is a man who expects people to live up to their commitments, to produce what they say they will -- that's how HE does things," said a Philips source, requesting anonimity.

That is a message that has already filtered through to the markets. "He has a well known style that he's somebody with a short fuse, if things can't be solved in the forseable future they have to change," said Eric de Graaf of ING Barings.

First up for attention could be Philips' management lines. "Philips still has a culture where people who know each other very well work closely together. That may be good in some ways but it can lead to unreceptiveness," the Philips source said.
Boonstra has no life-long Philips history, having worked for Unilever and headed the U.S. Sara Lee Corp, before joining Philips in 1994 -- and this could be an advantage, say analysts.

"He's not a Philips man. Maybe it brings a fresh approach. He's come from a background at Sara Lee that's strong on brand names, pretty good on restructuring -- all things that are relevant for Philips," said Morgan Stanley's Dean.
"His main strength is that he has a fresh view because he cames from outside. That's unique, he's the very first chairman from outside," said Van Beek.
"Another major strength is that he was bred in marketing-related jobs. That's still one of their (Philips) weaker spots although it has improved," he added.
But if Boonstra is to shake up the markets' perception of Philips and galvanise the share price back to the 83.90 guilder high of last year, he has to find new markets and approaches.

Alliances and cooperations are going to be the keys to unlock markets in the future, as technologies such as DVD -- the high capacity storage disc which can hold feature length movies -- and opportunities on the InterNet unfold.

Philips, bruised in the 1980s by losing out in a video recorder standard battle with the Japanese, can no longer afford to strike off on its own with new developments such as its Digital Compact Cassette or CD-Interactive, say analysts.

"It's not something you can force, but what I need is the feeling that he's willing to look for more compromise over alliances to make sure that new products are established," said Van Meer James Capel's Van Beek.
"He has to think about what is Philips trying to do. Get the business in shape. We need to complete what Timmer started and we need to find a growth strategy," said Dean.
"You can't sit around, you have to position yourself to maximise the benefits from areas you're capable of exploiting, which I think is the worry that they haven't been doing.
"Good companies don't wait for it to happen. Good companies in technology are spotting the next area and going for it," she said. -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
